title: Chapter 69: Fire at the Edge, Part 5 of 5: To the Edge
html:
They ran north.
All of them. The whole of Last Thorn. Out of the burning camp, over the bare ground behind the last tents, past the torn tent, past the big black thorn tree, and up the gravel slope of the ridge. Up and over it. In the dark. With the fire behind them, roaring, and the smoke rolling after them on the south wind, and the ticking coming on through the smoke.
Lyra ran with them.
She had a child in her arms. She did not know whose. A small one, a girl, in a fur, crying. Somebody had put her there. She ran with her, up the slope, slipping in the loose gravel in her felt-wrapped feet, with her sword in her other hand and her breath tearing in her throat.
There were people all round her in the dark. Women with babies. Old men being half carried. Boys driving goats in front of them with sticks, the goats leaping and bleating, scattering up the slope. Brin, limping, with his arm hanging, and Oda beside him holding him up. Marrit, the old woman, walking, not running, very straight, with her pole, as if she were going to market. Children everywhere, carried, dragged, running. And Kestrel's voice, over all of it, high and clear like a bell, calling, calling, keeping them together, keeping them going.
North. To the Edge.
At the top of the ridge Lyra looked back. She could not help it.
Last Thorn was burning.
All of it, now. Every tent. The whole bowl of ground between the thorn slope and the ridge was one great sheet of fire, red and yellow and orange, with the black ribs of the tent frames standing up out of it and falling, one by one, and the sparks going up into the dark in great whirling clouds, higher than the thorn trees, higher than the ridge. The light of it lay on the snow of the slope above, and on the faces round her, and on the smoke. She could feel the heat of it on her face from here. Even from here.
And the gray tent, the big one in the middle, Kestrel's tent, the tent of hands, was going. She saw it. A great dome of flame. And then the frame gave, and it fell in on itself, and was gone, all those hands, hundreds of them, gray on gray, into the fire.
And through the fire, black against it, three shapes. Walking. North. Out of the burning camp, toward the ridge. Toward them.
Ticking.
She turned and ran on, down the north side of the ridge.
The ground changed. She felt it at once, under her feet, even in the dark. On the south side of the ridge it had been gravel and frozen earth. Here, on the north side, going down the long mile of slope toward the Edge, it was snow. Old snow. Gray in the light of the fire behind them. And soft.
Not powder. Not the dry squeaking snow of the valleys. Rotten snow. Wet underneath. With a thin crust on top that broke under her feet at every step, so that she went through it to the ankle, and then to the shin, into a wet cold slush underneath.
The Glass, she thought. The warmth of it, coming up the slope. Melting the snow from underneath, all day, every day, until it was only a crust over water.
It was hard going. Her legs ached. The child in her arms was heavy. Around her, everyone was floundering, breaking through, falling, getting up. But they were light. They were people. The crust held them, mostly, for a step or two before it broke.
And behind them, on the ridge, the ticking stopped.
Not stopped. Changed. Slowed.
Lyra looked back again.
The three Erasers had come over the crest of the ridge. She could see them against the glow of the burning camp. Three black shapes, iron-dark, standing on the top of the ridge by the big black thorn tree, ten paces apart, the way they always were.
And then they came down the north side, onto the snow.
And went through it.
The first one took one step onto the rotten crust, and its iron foot went through as if the snow were not there. Down. Through the crust and the slush and the water underneath. To the knee. It stopped. Stood there for a moment, sunk to the knee in the snow, ticking. Then it lifted the foot, slowly, with a great sucking sound of slush, and put it forward, and the next foot went through too. To the knee.
The others were the same.
They were too heavy. Iron and brass, man-high, heavier than three men each. The crust that held a child for two steps could not hold them for one. At every step, they broke through. And sank. And had to drag themselves out. And sank again.
They came on. They did not stop. They never stopped. But they came on slowly. So slowly. Step, and sink, and drag. Step, and sink, and drag. Ticking.
Lyra heard someone laugh.
It was Arran. Somewhere ahead of her in the dark. A short sharp bark of a laugh, one only, wild and cracked, like a dog that has been kicked and is too surprised to whimper.
"The snow," he shouted back. "The snow's got them. The Glass is helping. Run."
They ran. Down the long slope. Through the rotten snow. The child in Lyra's arms had stopped crying. She was holding on to Lyra's collar with both fists, very tight, and looking back over Lyra's shoulder, at the fire, and the three black shapes.
The slope flattened out.
The snow got thinner, and wetter, and softer, and there were patches where there was no snow at all, only wet gravel and stones. And under Lyra's feet she began to hear water. Running. Little threads of it, in the dark, trickling between the stones, all going the same way. North. Down. In the light from the fire behind them they shone like silver wire.
And the warmth.
She felt it on her face, coming toward her out of the dark ahead. Dry and steady and faintly prickling. The breath of an oven door. The hum, coming up through the soles of her feet, through the felt, into her bones.
And then the people in front of her stopped.
All of them. All at once. In a long ragged line, in the dark, at the bottom of the slope.
And Lyra came up behind them, and stopped too, and stood with the child in her arms, breathing hard, and looked down.
The snow stopped.
It stopped in a line. A clean straight line, as if someone had cut it with a knife. On one side of the line, under her feet, there was the last of the snow, gray and wet and rotten, with the meltwater running out from under it in bright threads. On the other side, a step away, there was nothing.
No snow. No stones. No ground.
Glass.
Black. Smooth. Shining. Going out from the line, flat, into the dark, forever. With the stars in it.
The Edge.
Counting
Kestrel counted them.
She did it the way the Ashborn did everything, without fuss. She walked along the line at the Edge, slowly, from one end to the other, in the dark, and stopped at every family, and said names. And people answered. Here. Here. Here. A mother holding up a baby so she could see it. An old man lifting his stick. A child calling out in a high thin voice from somewhere in the crowd, here, here, I'm here.
Lyra stood and listened. She could not help counting too. She did not know the names, but she counted the answers. Twenty. Forty. Sixty. More.
Kestrel came to the end of the line, and stood there, and was quiet.
Then she said one more name.
Nobody answered.
She said it again. Louder. Into the dark.
Nobody answered.
A woman somewhere in the crowd made a sound. Not a scream. Something lower. And another woman went to her and held her.
"Ennis," said Arran, beside Lyra, very low. He had come up beside her without her seeing. His face was black with soot and his eyebrows were gone, singed off, so that he looked strange, younger, like a boy. "Old Ennis. He kept the goats. He went back for them. When the pen broke. I saw him go. Into the smoke. With his stick." He swallowed. "I shouted. He didn't hear."
Lyra did not say anything.
Kestrel stood at the end of the line for a long moment, with her face turned south, toward the glow beyond the ridge. Then she touched the gray line on her face. Slowly. The whole length of it. And bowed her head.
"We cannot breathe him," Arran said. Even lower. "There's nothing to breathe. He went in the fire. On his own. With nobody near." His voice cracked. "That's the worst way. For us. To go with nobody. Nobody to carry you. You just... go out. Like a lamp."
Lyra thought of Old Hask, saying goodbye to Vivienne in the dark. Somebody should.
"Then somebody should say goodbye to him," she said.
Arran looked at her.
Then he lifted his chin and called out, across the dark, toward the fire. One word. In the round Ashborn speech. Lyra thought it was the old man's name, and something after it. And then the woman who had made the sound called it too. And then Kestrel. And then all of them, the whole line, softly, one after another, saying it toward the ridge. Goodbye, Ennis. Goodbye. Goodbye.
It was not carrying. But it was something.
Then Vespera was there, small and sharp, pushing through the crowd with her rope belt clinking, going to Brin.
The big man was sitting on the wet gravel with his left arm hanging at a wrong angle from his shoulder, and his face gray with pain. Vespera knelt beside him and ran her blue fingers over the shoulder, quickly, the way she would have run them over a face she was about to paint. Brin grunted.
"Not broken," said Vespera. "Out. The joint's come out of its cup." She looked round. "Captain. You've done this before, I expect."
"Once or twice," said Oren.
He came and sat down on the gravel beside Brin, and took off his boot, and put his stockinged foot in the big man's armpit, and took Brin's wrist in both his hands. He said something to Brin in a low steady voice that Lyra could not hear. Brin nodded.
And Oren pulled.
There was a sound. A thick wet click, like a cork coming out of a bottle. Brin made a noise through his teeth, a long low groan. And then he let his breath out, and his gray face went slack, and he moved his arm. Slowly. Up. Down. It moved.
He looked at Oren. He said something.
"He says," said Arran, "you're the strongest man he's ever met, and he still wants to fight you with sticks when his arm's better."
Oren put his boot back on.
"Tell him any time," he said. "Tell him I'll let him win."
Arran told him. Brin laughed. A big, deep, surprised laugh, out there on the edge of the world, with the camp burning behind them and the ticking coming down the slope. And some of the others laughed too. Not much. A little.
And Kestrel came back down the line.
She stopped by Lyra and Corin and Oren and Vespera, and the five who were going. Arran. Brin, holding his arm. Oda, with her spear. Sef, with his singed hair. Marrit, with her pole.
"The families go east," she said. "Along the Edge. To the Salt Wells. There is a camp there, of our cousins. Two days. They will take them in." She did not look at the fire. "They will not follow the families. The iron. It does not want the families. It wants him." She looked at Corin. "It has only ever wanted him."
Corin did not say anything.
"So the families go east," said Kestrel. "And we go north. Tonight. Now. Not tomorrow." She looked at the black shining Glass, one step away. "We will not sleep on the Edge with that coming down the hill."
Nobody argued.
There was nothing to argue with.
Lyra looked down at her sword. At the notch near the guard, and the smear of black oil on the blade. She wiped it on the wet snow, slowly, both sides, the way Oren had taught her to wipe a blade when she was ten. The oil would not come off. It left a dull dark stain on the steel, like a bruise.
She put the sword away anyway.
Then she went and picked up her pack from the heap on the gravel, and her three water skins, and her felt-wrapped stone, still warm, and put them on. They were very heavy. Her arms, after two hundred and one swings of a thorn stick and one cut that had gone through iron, could hardly lift them.
She lifted them.
What Did You Give
Someone took the child out of her arms. A woman. Lyra did not see her face. Just a pair of hands, reaching, and a voice in the round Ashborn speech, and then the weight was gone and her arms were empty and light, so light that they floated up a little on their own.
She stood on the last of the snow.
All round her, in the dark, the people of Last Thorn were stopping. Gathering. Along the Edge, in a long ragged line, on the wet gravel and the last rotten snow, with the Glass one step in front of them. Counting each other. Calling names. Mothers finding children. Somebody was crying, loud. Somebody else was laughing, the way people laugh when they have not died. The goats were everywhere, bleating, wading in the meltwater.
And the packs.
Lyra saw them, in a heap on the gravel, a little way along. The walkers' packs. The water skins, three to a walker, sloshing. The hard bread in its bundles. The ten felt-wrapped stones, still warm. Arran and Sef had carried them. They had been stacked by the north tent since the afternoon, ready, and when the fire came the two of them had gone back for them, through the smoke, while everyone else ran. Sef's hair was singed. Arran's eyebrows were gone.
She did not know what to feel about that. She did not feel anything. She was too tired.
She looked down at her feet.
At the felt bags tied round her boots, gray and wet and filthy. At the last of the snow under them. At the clean straight line, a step away, where the snow stopped and the Glass began.
And she thought: I could dance here. On the snow. By the Edge. Just one step. Just to see.
She did not know why she thought it. She only knew she wanted to know.
She lifted her right foot.
One, two, three. And lift. And turn.
She tried.
And her feet did not know it.
That was the strange thing. That was what she could not explain, even to herself. She knew what she was trying to do. She knew the words of it. One, two, three, and lift, and turn. She could say them. She could think them. She could see, in her head, the shape of the thing, the way you can see the shape of a word on a page.
But her feet did not know it. Not at all. Her right foot went out, and stopped, and did not know where to go. Her left foot did not know when. There was no one, there was no two, there was no three. There was just a girl standing on wet snow with one foot in the air, like a heron, not knowing what to do with it.
She put the foot down. Wrong. On the edge of a stone. It turned under her.
And she fell.
Not far. She did not hit the ground. An arm caught her. A gray arm, in a charred and smoking sleeve. Round her waist. Hard. And held her up.
Corin.
He was standing beside her on the last of the snow, on his stiff leg, without his crutch. His face was black with soot. His hair was singed. His coat was burned through at both cuffs and there was a long black scorch mark down one side of it. He was breathing hard. And his gray arm was round her, holding her up, and she could feel it through her coat, hard and cold, like the arm of a statue.
She got her feet under her.
He did not let go at once.
"What did you give?" he said.
Very low. Close to her ear. In the dark.
She did not answer at once. She stood with his arm round her and looked at the Glass, black and shining, a step away.
She thought of lying to him. She did not know why. It would have been easy. Nothing. A face. A word. Something small. He would not have known.
No lies. That was the first rule. It was on the first page of his book, in his own hand.
"Dancing," she said.
His arm went still round her.
"My mother taught me," said Lyra. Her voice did not sound like her own. It sounded very small and very flat, like Gideon's. "In the hall at Crown Walk. When I was little. I'd forgotten I had it. And then tonight it came back. With the drums. And the flute. And I danced, and I..." She stopped. "And then the children were at the bread rack. And it was the nearest thing. It was right at the top. It was the warmest one I had."
She looked down at her feet. At the felt bags on the wet snow.
"So it went," she said. "It's gone. I can't..." She tried to move her foot. One, two, three. Nothing. "I can't even think how it went. I know it went one, two, three. I know there was a turn. But my feet don't know. They don't know any of it." She swallowed. "I'll never dance again. Not ever. Not at a ball. Not anywhere."
Corin did not say anything for a long moment.
Then he said, very quietly:
"I heard it."
She turned her head and looked at him.
"I heard it," said Corin. "Your happy voice. Just before. When you were dancing." His face in the faint light from the burning camp, far behind them over the ridge, was very still. "I've got it. I wrote it down. I've got it in me and on paper. Both."
Lyra looked at him.
At his black soot-smeared face. At his singed hair. At his wet eyes. At his gray arm, still round her.
And something happened in her chest. Something cracked open. Not grief. Not quite. Something else. Something that was almost like laughing.
"Then one of us has it," she said.
And he looked at her, and she saw that he understood. Not the words. Not exactly. The thing under the words. That she had given away the dance, and it was gone, and it was never coming back. And that the last time she had ever done it, the very last time, somebody had been watching. Somebody had heard what it sounded like. And kept it.
One of us has it.
He did not say anything. He took his arm from round her waist, slowly, as if he were not sure she would stand.
She stood.
And then, because she did not know what else to do with her hands, she put one of them, gloved, on his gray arm. Where it had been round her. Just for a moment. And took it away again.
Three
They stood at the Edge and watched Last Thorn burn.
All of them. The whole camp. In a long ragged line on the last of the snow, with their backs to the Glass.
Lyra noticed that. She noticed it the way you notice a clock stop. Every one of the Ashborn, in the whole long line, stood with their back to the Glass. For the first time since she had come over the Lip. Kestrel too. Arran too. Old Marrit, leaning on her pole. All of them. Facing south. Toward the fire. Toward the long dark slope going up to the ridge, and the red glow above it, where their tents were, and their bread, and their goats' pen, and their handprints.
Tonight they did not look at the Glass.
Tonight the Glass could look at them.
The fire had passed its worst. Lyra could see that, even from here, a mile off, over the dark line of the ridge. It was not a sheet of flame anymore. It was a glow. A deep red glow lying in the bowl of ground beyond the ridge, like the embers of a great hearth, with here and there a flame still licking up, yellow, and falling back. The sparks had stopped. The smoke went up in a long slow column, black against the stars, and leaned south on the wind, away from them, the way all the smoke at Last Thorn had always leaned.
As if even the smoke did not want to come to the Glass.
The big black thorn tree on the crest of the ridge stood out against the glow. Alone. Its twisted branches all reaching south. It had not burned. Lyra did not know how. Perhaps it was too old to burn. Perhaps it had stood there so long, trying to walk away from the Glass, that nothing could touch it now.
Nobody spoke.
And then Kestrel began to sing.
Very low. Lyra hardly heard it at first. It came from somewhere along the line to her left, in the dark, a low hoarse voice, hardly louder than breathing. Not a tune. Not quite. Something between a tune and a hum. A long slow line of sound that went down, and down, and stayed down, like a stone sinking in deep water.
Then another voice took it up. A woman's. And another. And then the men. Low. All of them. Along the whole length of the line, in the dark, at the Edge. The Ashborn of Last Thorn, singing to their tents. Lyra did not know the words. There might not have been words. It did not matter. She knew what it was. It was the sound you make for the dead. For the ones you carry. For the things you have lost and will not get back.
For the tents, with all their hands.
She found she was crying. Quietly. She did not wipe it away.
Beside her Corin stood on his stiff leg, leaning on his crutch. Oren had picked it up off the gravel by the big fire as they ran, without a word, and carried it out of the burning camp under his arm with a child on his other shoulder, and given it back to him at the Edge. Now Corin leaned on it with one hand and on Oren's shoulder with the other, and Oren was letting him. Oren's face in the red glow was hard and set, and his notched sword was in his hand, point down on the gravel. And on Oren's other side Vespera stood very small, wrapped in her fur, with her rope belt of needles round her waist and her blue hands folded in front of her, singing too. Low. In the Ashborn way. As if she had learned it a long time ago and never forgotten.
Corin was not singing. He was writing.
Lyra saw him. He had the green book out, on his knee, and the stub of his pencil, and he was bending over it in the red light of the far fire, close, and writing. She did not look at what. She did not need to. She knew what it would say.
She would read it later. When he let her.
The singing went on. Down, and down, and down.
And under it, behind it, through it, very faint, from somewhere up the long dark slope between the Edge and the ridge, there was another sound.
Lyra closed her eyes.
She listened. Not to the singing. Under the singing. The way she had listened to her father's breathing in the last hours, counting, four thousand breaths and more, from the first bell to the end. The way she listened to everything. Counting.
Tick.
There.
Tick. Tick.
Far off. Up the slope. In the dark. In the rotten snow. Slow. Very slow. Step, and sink, and drag. Step, and sink, and drag. But coming. Not stopped. Never stopped. Coming down the long slope from the ridge toward the Edge, toward them, at the slow terrible patient pace of something that never gets tired.
She counted.
Not the ticks. The voices. The separate sounds, under the singing. Each one its own clock. Each one a little out of time with the others, and then falling into time.
One.
She listened.
Two.
She listened harder. With her eyes shut and her face wet and the Ashborn singing round her and the warm breath of the Glass on the back of her neck, one step behind her.
Three.
She waited for four.
Four did not come.
Four was lying on its face in the ashes of the bread rack, among the scattered loaves, with a ragged hole in its back and a small folded square stamped on the brass of its heart. Four was broken. She had broken it. With her mother's dance.
One. Two. Three.
Lyra opened her eyes.
The singing had stopped. The Ashborn were silent along the Edge. They had heard it too.
Kestrel turned round. Away from the fire. Toward the Glass. And the others, one by one, all along the line, turned with her.
Lyra turned too.
And there it was. A step in front of her. Black, and smooth, and shining, and warm, going out into the dark forever, with all the stars of the sky lying in it.
Behind her, up the slope, the ticking came on.
Three.
